final_proof:
We prove the identity by a Fourier-series argument, including the convergence justification.

First, we establish the form of the Dirichlet convergence theorem that we need. If a 2π-periodic function f is piecewise C¹, then its Fourier series at x converges to (f(x−)+f(x+))/2. Indeed, if S_N f(x) is its N-th Fourier partial sum, the Dirichlet-kernel formula gives

S_N f(x) = (1/(2π)) ∫_{−π}^{π} f(x−t) [sin((N+1/2)t)/sin(t/2)] dt.

The Dirichlet kernel has integral 2π over [−π,π]. Splitting the integral at zero, using its evenness, and subtracting the appropriate one-sided limits therefore gives

S_N f(x) − (f(x−)+f(x+))/2
= (1/(2π)) ∫_0^π [(f(x−t)−f(x−))+(f(x+t)−f(x+))]/sin(t/2) · sin((N+1/2)t) dt,

where the arguments of f are read modulo 2π. The quotient multiplying the final sine is integrable on (0,π): near zero, the existence of the relevant one-sided derivatives makes its numerator O(t), while sin(t/2) is asymptotic to t/2; away from zero, piecewise continuity suffices. Its oscillatory integral tends to zero by the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma. In the special form used here, that lemma follows by approximating an integrable piecewise-continuous function in L¹ by step functions: the integral of any step function times sin(λt) tends to zero as |λ| tends to infinity, and the L¹-approximation controls the remaining integral uniformly in λ. This proves the stated convergence theorem.

Now let f(x)=x² on [−π,π], extended 2π-periodically. Write its Fourier series in the form

f(x) ~ a₀/2 + Σ_{n=1}^∞ (a_n cos(nx)+b_n sin(nx)).

Because f is even, b_n=0. Also,

a₀ = (1/π)∫_{−π}^{π}x² dx = 2π²/3.

For every integer n≥1, two integrations by parts yield

a_n = (2/π)∫_0^π x² cos(nx) dx
= (2/π)(−2/n)∫_0^π x sin(nx) dx
= (2/π)(−2/n)([−x cos(nx)/n]_0^π + (1/n)∫_0^π cos(nx) dx)
= 4(−1)^n/n².

Thus the Fourier series of f is

x² ~ π²/3 + 4Σ_{n=1}^∞ (−1)^n cos(nx)/n².

At x=π, the left-hand limit of the periodic extension is π², and the right-hand limit is the limit of x² as x approaches −π from the right, which is also π². The convergence theorem therefore says that the series at x=π converges to π². Since cos(nπ)=(−1)^n, we obtain

π² = π²/3 + 4Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n².

Consequently,

Σ_{n=1}^∞ 1/n² = (1/4)(π²−π²/3) = π²/6.

By the definition ζ(s)=Σ_{n=1}^∞ n^(−s) for real s>1, the sum on the left is ζ(2). Hence ζ(2)=π²/6.
